items.meta_title: Run VpnHood! SERVER in Docker | VpnHood!
items.meta_description: Run VpnHood! SERVER as a Docker container on Linux with one command, managed from VpnHood! MANAGER or standalone. The container keeps the server up to date.
items.title: Run VpnHood! SERVER in Docker
items.lead: Run the server as a container on any Linux machine with Docker. One command installs it, as a managed server or a standalone one, and the container keeps the server running and up to date.
items.req_machine: A Linux machine with a public IP address, on x64 or arm64. The image is built for both.
items.req_docker: Docker with its compose plugin. The installer can install it for you on Ubuntu, Debian and the distributions based on them.
items.req_port: TCP port [server_port] open, both in the machine's firewall and in your hosting provider's. The container shares the host's network, so the server listens on the host's port directly.
items.mgr_command: In VpnHood! MANAGER, open [manager_servers], select [manager_add], name the server and select [manager_create]. Among the ways to install it, choose [manager_install_command]. In the command MANAGER shows, change [installer_linux] to [installer_docker], then run it on the machine. It installs the container with the settings that connect the server to MANAGER, and asks the question the standalone install below asks.
items.mgr_existing: For a container you created already, choose [manager_install_manual] instead. Save the settings MANAGER shows as [server_appsettings] on the host, then restart the container with [docker_restart].
items.mgr_keys: Then create the access keys for your devices in MANAGER, under [manager_access_tokens].
items.step_install_run: Run this command. It downloads the compose file, starts the server's container and asks you one question.
items.step_install_docker: When it asks [docker_prompt], type [answer_yes] to have Docker installed, or [answer_no] if the machine has it already.
items.caption_unattended: In a script, install without the question. Leave out [flag_install_docker] if Docker is installed already.
items.step_install_storage: The server keeps its settings, keys and logs in [server_storage] on the host, so they outlive the container.
items.step_key_run: Run this on the machine. The key is made inside the server's container, so it uses the server's own settings.
items.step_key_same: The output and the options are the same as for a standalone server installed without Docker: copy the line under [accesskey_heading], and see Create your first access key for the options that limit a key.
items.caption_example: For example, a key for one phone
items.step_connect: Install VpnHood! CLIENT on each device, add the key, and connect.
items.manage_title: Start, stop and check the server
items.manage_desc: The container is called [docker_container]. Docker starts it again when the machine restarts, and inside it the server is started again if it crashes.
items.manage_log: The same log is written to [server_log] on the host.
items.settings_file: The server reads its settings from [server_appsettings]. Edit the file, then restart the container with [docker_restart].
items.settings_env: Where you cannot edit a file, put the whole content of an appsettings.json in the [env_appsettings] environment variable instead. The server then uses it in place of the file.
items.settings_more: Set your server's IP addresses and Connect through a domain name walk through the settings you are most likely to change.
items.updates_auto: The server updates itself inside the container. It checks for a new release when it starts and every 12 hours, and restarts into the new version.
items.updates_off: To stay on one version, set [env_auto_update_off] in the container's environment.
items.updates_image: Now and then a release needs a newer image. The server then keeps its current version, and its log says [log_pull_image] Run the install command again: it pulls the latest image and creates the container again, with the same settings and keys.
items.updates_old: If you installed with an earlier version of the script, run the install command again. It moves the server to the new image and removes the old [old_updater_container] container.
items.manual_desc: If you manage your containers by hand, this is the container the installer creates. Run it on the host's network, as the installer does.
items.manual_update: To move it to a newer image, pull [docker_image] and create the container again.
